simple: the program that shares the computer fairly between all the other programs and does the risky jobs for them.
analogy: the school principal and the timetable.
precise: the software that manages a computer's hardware resources (processor time, memory, storage, devices) and provides programs with abstractions of them (processes, address spaces, files) and a controlled interface to them (system calls).
source: D1 of F3-01 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D2 of F3-01 ("xv6: a simple, Unix-like teaching operating system") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the operating system that runs with full power over the machine.
analogy: the principal's office and its staff.
precise: the part of the OS that executes in the processor's privileged mode, handles every system call, exception and interrupt, and owns the page tables, the scheduler and the device drivers. Not the same as a GPU kernel (the function every GPU thread runs, F6).
source: D2 of F3-01 ("xv6: a simple, Unix-like teaching operating system"); D3 of F3-01 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two levels of permission the processor itself enforces: ordinary programs run with few permissions, the kernel with all of them.
analogy: student areas and staff-only rooms.
precise: processor privilege levels; code in user mode cannot execute privileged instructions or touch memory and devices it has not been granted, and enters the kernel only through traps (system calls, exceptions, interrupts). The names differ by architecture (x86 rings, RISC-V U/S/M modes, Arm exception levels).
source: D1 of F3-01 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D5 of F3-01 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a program while it is running, with its own memory and its own number.
analogy: a class with its own room.
precise: the OS's abstraction of a running program: an address space, one or more threads of execution, and kernel-held state such as open files and a process identifier (PID). F3-02 treats it in depth.
source: D1 of F3-01 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D3 of F3-01 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a request from a program to the kernel, such as "write these bytes" or "give me more memory".
analogy: asking at the office window with a form.
precise: a controlled entry into the kernel: the program places a call number and arguments in agreed registers and executes a trap instruction; the kernel checks the request, performs it in kernel mode and returns a result (or an error number) to user mode. F3-07 treats it in depth.
source: D1 of F3-01 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D3 of F3-01 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tool that prints every system call a program makes.
analogy: a notebook kept at the office window, listing every form handed in and the answer given.
precise: a Linux diagnostic utility that uses the kernel's process-tracing interface to stop a traced process at each system-call entry and exit and print the call, its decoded arguments and its return value (or error name).
source: D6 of F3-01 (strace(1) manual page, strace project); R2 of F3-01 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a system call that makes the program wait until something happens, such as input arriving.
analogy: a class waiting for a book from the library: the teacher teaches another class meanwhile.
precise: the behaviour of a system call that cannot complete at once (for example read with no data available): the kernel marks the calling thread blocked, runs other threads, and makes it ready again when the event occurs; the call then returns its result.
source: D1 of F3-01 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); R4 of F3-01 (lab run in this build: a read that waits) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number the kernel gives each process.
analogy: the class's register number.
precise: a positive integer that names a process in system calls such as waitpid and kill; getpid returns the caller's, getppid its parent's.
source: D4 of F3-02 (Linux man-pages: getpid(2), fork(2), proc(5)); R1 of F3-02 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the kernel's record card for one process.
analogy: the class's file in the principal's cabinet.
precise: the kernel data structure holding a process's state, saved registers (when it is not running), memory map, open files, PID, parent and exit status; xv6 calls it struct proc.
source: D1 of F3-02 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D2 of F3-02 (the xv6 book (RISC-V edition)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the call that makes a copy of the running process.
analogy: splitting a class into two identical classes in two rooms.
precise: a POSIX system call that creates a child process whose address space and open files are copies of the caller's; it returns twice: 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent (−1 on failure, with no child).
source: D3 of F3-02 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D4 of F3-02 (Linux man-pages: fork(2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the call that replaces the running program with a different one, in the same process.
analogy: the class keeps its room and number but swaps every book for a new subject.
precise: the execve system call (and its C library front ends such as execv) loads a new program image into the calling process, keeping its PID and (by default) its open files; on success it does not return.
source: D3 of F3-02 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D4 of F3-02 (Linux man-pages: execve(2), exec(3)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the call a parent uses to wait for a child to finish and hear how it ended.
analogy: signing the attendance sheet.
precise: system calls that block the caller until a child changes state (by default, terminates), return the child's PID and store a status word decoded with WIFEXITED and WEXITSTATUS; collecting it lets the kernel free the child's remaining record.
source: D4 of F3-02 (Linux man-pages: wait(2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the small number a program hands back when it ends: 0 for success.
analogy: the mark written on the attendance sheet.
precise: the value passed to exit or returned from main, of which the parent receives the low 8 bits through wait; by convention 0 means success.
source: D3 of F3-02 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); D4 of F3-02 (Linux man-pages: wait(2), _exit(2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a process that has finished but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status.
analogy: an unsigned attendance sheet on the principal's desk.
precise: a terminated process whose kernel record (PID, exit status, resource usage) is kept until its parent waits for it; it uses no CPU or user memory, but its process-table entry and PID stay taken.
source: D3 of F3-02 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective"); R4 of F3-02 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what a process is doing right now: running, ready to run, waiting, or finished.
analogy: a class being taught, waiting for a teacher, waiting for the library, or gone home.
precise: the kernel's classification of a process for scheduling: running (on a CPU), ready (runnable, waiting for a CPU), blocked (waiting for an event such as I/O), plus states for creation and termination such as zombie.
source: D1 of F3-02 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the kernel stops one thread, saves where it was, and starts another.
analogy: the teacher leaves a bookmark in the register, packs up and goes to the next room.
precise: the kernel operation that saves the registers (including the program counter and stack pointer) of the running thread into its kernel record, restores another thread's saved registers and, if the new thread belongs to another process, switches to that process's page tables.
source: D1 of F3-03 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D2 of F3-03 (the xv6 book (RISC-V edition)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the kernel that decides which thread runs next, and for how long.
analogy: the timetable.
precise: the kernel component that selects, from the ready threads, the next one to run on each CPU, according to a scheduling policy, whenever a thread blocks, exits, or is preempted.
source: D1 of F3-03 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: taking the CPU away from a thread that has not finished.
analogy: the bell rings and the teacher must go, even mid-sentence.
precise: the scheduler's ability to stop a running thread, normally on a timer interrupt, and make it ready again so that another thread can run; a policy that never does this is non-preemptive.
source: D1 of F3-03 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long a thread may run before the scheduler may take the CPU away.
analogy: the length of one lesson period.
precise: the maximum interval a thread runs before a round-robin scheduler preempts it and moves it to the back of the ready queue.
source: D1 of F3-03 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long a job takes from arriving to finishing.
analogy: from the moment a class asks for the teacher until its lesson is done.
precise: Tturnaround = Tcompletion − Tarrival.
source: D1 of F3-03 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long a job waits before it first gets the CPU.
analogy: how long a class waits before the teacher first walks in.
precise: Tresponse = Tfirst run − Tarrival.
source: D1 of F3-03 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a job that never gets the CPU because others are always chosen first.
analogy: a class always moved down the timetable because more urgent classes keep arriving.
precise: indefinite postponement of a ready thread by a scheduling policy, for example strict priority with a steady supply of higher-priority work.
source: D7 of F3-03 ("Operating System Concepts") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: letting a job become more urgent the longer it waits.
analogy: the longer a class has waited, the higher it moves on the timetable.
precise: a technique that gradually raises the effective priority of threads that have waited a long time, bounding how long any ready thread can be postponed.
source: D7 of F3-03 ("Operating System Concepts") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one page-sized piece of real memory.
analogy: one real cupboard.
precise: a page-aligned block of physical memory, of the page size, that the kernel can map at one or more virtual pages; identified by its physical page number (PPN).
source: D1 of F3-04 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: giving a program real memory only when it first touches it.
analogy: "no cupboard yet" until the locker is first opened.
precise: a policy in which the kernel records that a virtual range is valid but maps no frame until the first access faults; the fault handler then allocates (or reads in) the page and maps it.
source: D1 of F3-04 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: after fork, parent and child share the same memory until one of them writes, and only then is a private copy made.
analogy: two classes share one cupboard for reading; the first class to put something in gets its own cupboard.
precise: a technique in which pages are mapped read-only into several address spaces; a write causes a page fault, and the handler copies the page, maps the copy writable for the writer, and restarts the write.
source: D1 of F3-04 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D3 of F3-04 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the RISC-V rule book for 39-bit virtual addresses.
analogy: the school's rule for writing locker maps as a three-level index.
precise: the RISC-V paged virtual-memory mode with 39-bit virtual addresses, 4 KiB pages and three levels of 512-entry page tables; the mode xv6 uses.
source: D5 of F3-04 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture"); D2 of F3-04 (the xv6 book (RISC-V edition)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a variable that says "somebody is using this data; wait".
analogy: the one key to a shared cupboard.
precise: a synchronization object with acquire and release operations that guarantees that at most one thread holds it at a time; code holding the lock forms a critical section. Also called a mutual-exclusion lock.
source: D1 of F3-05 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a lock whose waiters give up the CPU until it is free.
analogy: writing your name on the list and sitting down until you are called.
precise: a lock whose acquire operation, when the lock is taken, blocks the calling thread (the scheduler runs something else) and wakes it when the lock is released; suited to long critical sections. std::mutex is the C++ interface to one.
source: D1 of F3-05 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D8 of F3-05 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: RISC-V's word for one CPU that runs instructions.
analogy: one teacher.
precise: a RISC-V hardware thread: a context that fetches and executes its own instruction stream with its own registers; each has a number readable from the mhartid register.
source: D6 of F3-05 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged ISA"); D5 of F3-05 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the OS that keeps named files on a storage device.
analogy: the library catalogue and shelves.
precise: an on-disk data layout (allocation maps, inodes, directories, data blocks) together with the kernel code that implements files and names on top of a block device and keeps the layout consistent.
source: D1 of F3-06 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); S2 of F3-06 (University Authoring Guide, section 8.1, F3/F4 analogy map) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the record that describes one file, without its name.
analogy: a catalogue card: size and the shelves that hold the pages.
precise: an on-disk structure, identified by an inode number, holding a file's type, size, permissions, link count, timestamps and the addresses of its data blocks (directly or through indirect blocks).
source: D1 of F3-06 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D2 of F3-06 (the xv6 book (RISC-V edition)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a special file that lists names and the inodes they belong to.
analogy: a list of titles, each with a card number.
precise: a file whose content is a set of entries (name, inode number); path lookup reads directories one component at a time, starting at the root directory's inode.
source: D1 of F3-06 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one more name for a file that already exists.
analogy: two titles pointing to the same card.
precise: a directory entry; every name of a file is a hard link to its inode, the inode's link count records how many there are, and the file's storage is freed only when the count is 0 and no process has it open.
source: D1 of F3-06 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D4 of F3-06 (Linux man-pages: link(2), unlink(2), stat(2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making sure a power cut never leaves the file system in a state that lies.
analogy: shelving in an order that survives a power cut mid-way.
precise: the property that the on-disk structures, after a crash at any point of an update that touches several blocks, are either consistent or can be made consistent, without exposing other files' data; achieved by careful write ordering, journaling (logging) or copy-on-write.
source: D1 of F3-06 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tool that checks a file system's records against each other after a crash.
analogy: the librarian checks that every shelf marked "in use" belongs to some card.
precise: a file-system consistency checker that scans allocation maps, inodes and directories, and repairs disagreements (leaked blocks, wrong link counts, blocks used twice); it cannot tell whether a block holds the right data.
source: D1 of F3-06 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: writing a note of what you are about to change before changing it.
analogy: the librarian writes "card 2 → shelf 0, shelf 0 = new pages" in a notebook first, then shelves; after a power cut she redoes what the notebook says.
precise: a technique in which the blocks of an update are first written to a log on disk and committed with a final record; after a crash, committed transactions are replayed and uncommitted ones ignored, so the update is all-or-nothing.
source: D1 of F3-06 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D2 of F3-06 (the xv6 book (RISC-V edition)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the processor stops the program and jumps into the kernel.
analogy: the window opens and the clerk takes over.
precise: a synchronous or asynchronous transfer of control to a privileged handler, caused by a trap instruction (system call), an exception (fault) or an interrupt; the hardware records the cause and the interrupted program counter and raises the privilege level.
source: D1 of F3-07 ("Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D5 of F3-07 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the saved copy of the program's registers while the kernel works.
analogy: the clerk copies everything on the student's desk onto a tray, and puts it back afterwards.
precise: a memory area, written by the kernel's trap entry code, that holds the interrupted program's general-purpose registers, so that the handler can read the arguments, write the result and restore the program exactly.
source: D2 of F3-07 (the xv6 book (RISC-V edition)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the RISC-V instruction that asks the next privilege level for service.
analogy: sliding the form through the window.
precise: the RISC-V environment-call instruction; executed in user mode, it raises an exception with cause 8 ("environment call from U-mode") into the handler of a higher privilege level.
source: D6 of F3-07 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged ISA"); D5 of F3-07 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the RISC-V processor's most powerful mode, which can touch everything.
analogy: the principal's keys.
precise: the highest RISC-V privilege level (M), in which a hart starts after reset; below it are supervisor mode (S, where xv6 and Linux run) and user mode (U); the university's kernel uses only M and U.
source: D5 of F3-07 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: RISC-V hardware that says which physical addresses lower modes may use.
analogy: a fence around the student area of the building.
precise: a set of machine-mode registers (address and configuration pairs) that grant read, write and execute permission on physical address ranges to S and U mode; an access by those modes that no entry allows raises an access-fault exception.
source: D5 of F3-07 ("The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume II: Privileged Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number that says why a system call failed.
analogy: the reason stamped on a refused form.
precise: a thread-local variable that the C library sets from the error code a failing Linux system call returns (the call itself returns −1); for example EFAULT (14, "Bad address") and ENOSYS (38, "Function not implemented") on the build machine.
source: D4 of F3-07 (Linux man-pages: errno(3), syscall(2)); R1 of F3-07 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small Unix-like teaching operating system.
analogy: a model school built so pupils can see every room.
precise: a re-implementation of Sixth Edition Unix's ideas in C for multicore RISC-V (and earlier x86), written at MIT for teaching operating systems, with a book that explains its source; it runs in QEMU.
source: D2 of F3-08 (the xv6 book, RISC-V edition); D9 of F3-08 (xv6-riscv source code, MIT PDOS) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of function and variable names in a program file, with their addresses.
analogy: the building plan's room list.
precise: the section of an ELF file that maps names to addresses and kinds (code, data); printed by nm, used by debuggers and addr2line to turn addresses into names and source lines.
source: D3 of F3-08 ("Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list that turns a system-call number into the kernel function that handles it.
analogy: the binder at the office window: form number to procedure.
precise: an array of handler pointers indexed by system-call number, used by the kernel's dispatcher after a bounds check; its order must match the numbers that user programs are built with.
source: D2 of F3-08 (the xv6 book (RISC-V edition)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the tiny function a program calls, which puts the number in a register and traps.
analogy: the pre-printed form with the form number already filled in.
precise: a library function (in xv6, generated from a script; in uni-rv, the inline ecall wrapper) that loads the system-call number and arguments into the convention's registers and executes the trap instruction.
source: D2 of F3-08 (the xv6 book (RISC-V edition)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a program that runs your lab solution and says pass or fail.
analogy: the exam marker's checklist.
precise: in 6.1810, per-lab scripts run by the Makefile that boot xv6 in QEMU, run test programs, and compare their output with expected patterns; the curriculum's P4 acceptance is that they pass.
source: D10 of F3-08 (MIT 6.1810 lab pages); S1 of F3-08 (Systems Curriculum, milestone P4: "xv6 lab grading scripts pass.") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
